paragraphs.text: Taking too much responsibility means assuming more work, decision ownership or responsibility for other people’s feelings than is reasonably yours in an arrangement. That could mean repeatedly rescuing missed commitments or feeling obliged to prevent every disappointment. The question depends on real duties, capacity and circumstances, rather than a rule that helping less is always better.

Separate what is yours from what has become yours by default. Care, parenting, professional obligations and emergencies can involve substantial real responsibilities. An assumed duty to manage every outcome is different. A useful change protects essential needs while making ownership and support more realistic.

sections.title: Care and control can become entangled

paragraphs.text: You might step in from care, habit, fear of an outcome or a wish to retain control. Others may come to rely on that response, or may lack genuine alternative support. These possibilities do not prove that the helper created the problem. Heavy invisible work can also look small to someone who does not see its coordination.

Doing more can sometimes remove another person’s choices or opportunities without agreement. Someone may need assistance while still wanting to make a decision themselves. Ask what help is necessary and welcome, rather than assuming that your concern gives you ownership of the whole task or every result.

sections.title: Three research perspectives help ask questions

paragraphs.text: Jason Colquitt and colleagues combined studies of organisational fairness, distinguishing outcomes, procedures, treatment and information. Those distinctions can help examine an uneven workload. The evidence largely concerns organisations and cannot establish the correct division for every family or care arrangement, or prove dishonesty when people disagree.

Susan Michie and colleagues reviewed behaviour-change frameworks and proposed considering capability, opportunity and motivation together. Their framework is not a diagnostic test of why someone failed to act. Richard Ryan and Edward Deci reviewed autonomy, competence and connection in motivation. These ideas help identify questions about support and choice, rather than determining an individual motive.

sections.title: Map the work that actually happens

paragraphs.text: Choose one recurring task and identify its parts. Who agreed to own the decision, the preparation, the doing and the backup? What happens if you do not intervene? Include costs to your health and other responsibilities, as well as the needs of the person who depends on the work.

In a fictional work example, you repeatedly finish a shared report after a colleague misses their part. The deadline may genuinely need protection, yet your emergency help has become an invisible standing arrangement. Clarifying ownership and an earlier warning point can address that pattern without deciding whether the colleague intended to rely on you.

Renegotiate one responsibility with an owner, adequate resources, backup and a point for raising difficulty. Saying someone else now owns it is insufficient if they lack the necessary information, access or assistance. Make the transfer workable and review what happens. A sustainable plan needs more than a declaration that you are stepping back.

Do not abruptly abandon someone who depends on essential care. State what you can genuinely offer and seek relevant support for an unmanageable, exploitative or coercive arrangement. Self-sacrifice need not be the only proposed solution. At the same time, another adult’s disappointment does not always mean you have failed a real duty.

sections.title: Review needs as well as workload

paragraphs.text: Consider one task you repeatedly absorb. What did you agree to own, what became yours by default, and what support would make a safe change possible? Choose a transfer, limit or support request. Pause the player for longer if helpful.

A practical step might move the warning point earlier and identify who supplies backup, instead of leaving you to rescue the final hour. Later, review your workload, essential needs and whether the new arrangement actually functions. The aim is sustainable responsibility that preserves care and meaningful choice.
